{{Short description|1969 psychology article by Arthur Jensen}}
[[File:Arthur Jensen Vanderbilt 2002.jpg|300px|thumb|[[Arthur Jensen]]]]

"'''How Much Can We Boost IQ and Achievement?'''" is a 1969 article by the American psychologist [[Arthur Jensen]] published in the ''[[Harvard Educational Review]]''.<ref>Jensen (1969)</ref> 
Controversy over the article led to the coining of the term ''[[Jensenism]],''<ref>{{cite book |title=Intelligence, Race, and Genetics: Conversations with Arthur R. Jensen |year=2002 |first=Frank |last=Miele |authorlink=Frank Miele |chapter=Jensenism: A New Word in the Dictionary |at=kindle loc. 418-23 |publisher=Westview Press |isbn=0-8133-4274-0}}</ref> defined as the theory that [[IQ]] is largely determined by [[genes]], including [[racial heritage]].<ref>{{cite dictionary |year=1996 |entry=Jensenism |page=1026 |dictionary=Webster's New Universal Unabridged Dictionary |publisher=Barnes and Noble | isbn=0-7607-0288-8}}</ref> 
It is among the most controversial<ref>{{cite news|title=All Brains Are the Same Color |newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=9 December 2007|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/12/09/opinion/09nisbett.html|author=Richard E. Nisbett|access-date=25 December 2011}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Tucker|1996|p=201}}</ref> in American [[psychology]], and was largely responsible for initiating the current debate over [[race and intelligence]].<ref>{{harvnb|Hunt|Carlson|2007}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=Getting Smarter About IQ|journal=[[The American Prospect]]|date=16 April 2009|author=David Kirp}}</ref>

The article generated significant attention to,<ref>{{cite news|title=Genetics, IQ Study Proposed|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=4 March 1970|author=Austin Wehrwein|page=A3}}</ref> and protests against, Jensen's work.<ref>{{cite news|title=Harassment Charged by Author Of Article About Negroes' I.Q.'s|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=19 May 1969|author=Lawrence E. Davies|page=33}}</ref>

==Overview==

Jensen's argument consisted of a series of related claims.<ref>Loehlin, Lindzey and Spuhler (1975)</ref> [[IQ tests]] are valid measurements of a real human ability—what people generally describe as "intelligence"—that is important to many parts of contemporary life. Intelligence, as measured by IQ tests, is about 80 percent [[Heritability of IQ|heritable]]. Intelligent parents are much more likely to have intelligent children than other parents. Remedial educational programs have failed to raise the measured intelligence of individuals or groups. Indeed, one of the most inflammatory sentences is the opener: "Compensatory education has been tried and apparently has failed." The article generated extensive discussion and controversy both in the popular press<ref>{{harvnb|Tucker|1996|p=204}}</ref> and in the academic literature.<ref>Jencks and Phillips (1998)</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Book Review: Bias in Mental Testing|journal=Applied Psychological Measurement|date=July 1980|volume=4|number=3|editor=Susan Whitely|pages=403–406|doi=10.1177/014662168000400311|s2cid=119406346}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Johnson |first=Wendy |title=Developmental Psychology: Revisiting the Classic Studies |editor1-last=Slater |editor1-first=Alan M. |editor2-last=Quinn |editor2-first=Paul C. |chapter=How Much Can We Boost IQ? An Updated Look at Jensen's (1969) Question and Answer |location=Thousand Oaks, CA |publisher=SAGE |series=Psychology: Revisiting the Classic Studies |isbn=978-0-85702-757-3 |date=2012}}</ref> The article prompted 29 academic rebuttals, leading the journal to eventually decide to refuse reprints or allow Jensen to respond to critical letters.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://newint.org/features/2015/03/01/pseudo-science-dangerous |title=Race science rears its ugly head |last=Evans |first=Gavin |date=2015-03-01 |website=New Internationalist |language=en |access-date=2018-04-27}}</ref> Some college students also responded to the publication of the paper by burning effigies of Jensen and sending him death threats.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/11/02/science/arthur-r-jensen-who-set-off-debate-on-iq-dies.html |title=Arthur R. Jensen, Who Set Off Debate on I.Q., Dies |last=Fox |first=Margalit |date=2012-11-01 |work=The New York Times |access-date=2018-04-27 |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> 

In 1982, Schiff et al. conducted an adoption study that aimed to provide a direct answer to the question Jensen had posted in his 1969 paper. They reported that children who were adopted into families of a higher social class experienced, on average, "an increase of 14 IQ points in the mean IQ score estimated with 2 tests and a reduction by a factor of 4 in the probability of repeating a grade."<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schiff |first1=Michel |last2=Duyme |first2=Michel |last3=Dumaret |first3=Annick |last4=Tomkiewicz |first4=Stanislaw |date=September 1982 |title=How much could we boost scholastic achievement and IQ scores? A direct answer from a French adoption study |journal=Cognition |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=165–196 |doi=10.1016/0010-0277(82)90011-7 |pmid=6890431 |s2cid=40741672 |issn=0010-0277}}</ref>

Jensen's critics argue that most aspects of his analysis were flawed: [[IQ tests]] do not provide a stable or meaningful measure of intelligence; IQ is affected by the environment and not solely or mainly a function of genetics; there is no evidence for genetic differences in racial intelligence; and that the entire topic was too controversial to be productively discussed.<ref>{{cite news|title=Jensenism|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=31 August 1969|author=Lee Edson|page=SM10}}</ref>
